Photo by Damian Dovarganes, AP Photo In summary Supporters say California desperately needs money to fund housing construction and make a dent in its homelessness and affordability crisis. Critics say bond financing isn’t the way to do it. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. For years, California has grappled with a problem that has affected nearly every aspect of our society: The state doesn’t have enough homes that people can afford to live in. Proposition 1 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-1-housing-bond/) aims to address that crisis. It’s estimated that more than 180,000 Californians (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/05/point-in-time-homelessness-report/) are homeless. Rents are so high that a minimum wage worker would need to work 102 hours a week (https://nlihc.org/oor/state/ca) to afford a typical one-bedroom apartment, according to the National Low Income Housing Coalition. A big piece of that problem is construction: Not enough homes are being built. Fewer than a third (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/08/california-rhna-housing-affordable-progress/) of California cities and counties are on track to permit enough market-rate housing to hit their state-mandated targets, and fewer than 6% are on track for very low-income housing. Those targets are based on the state’s assumption that we need nearly 2.5 million more homes. Legislators have passed multiple laws (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/10/newsom-signs-massive-california-housing-overhaul/) trying to address that (https://calmatters.org/education/2026/10/new-laws-affordable-student-housing-california/) by making it easier, faster and cheaper to get projects permitted (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/06/ceqa-urban-development-infill-budget/) and built. Prop. 1 is supposed to supply the money. A recent report estimated (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/03/affordable-housing-bottleneck/) nearly 40,000 affordable units throughout California have been designed, permitted and partially funded and are sitting stalled because developers just can’t quite get enough money to build them. What would Prop. 1 do? If it passes, Prop. 1 would allow the state to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds to fund various types of housing, including homes for veterans, homeless Californians, renters, homeowners, farmworkers, students and tribes. Where would the money go? Prop. 1 would fund a variety of programs. Here’s how it breaks down: $7.2 billion to buy, build or renovate apartment buildings, generally through low-interest loans to developers. Projects funded this way would have to reserve a certain number of units for low-income households. Some would be used for “supportive housing,” homeless housing that includes additional services. This, in combination with other funding sources, would help support up to 40,000 rental units, according to (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop1-110326.pdf) the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office. $1.25 billion to help veterans secure loans to buy homes. $1.1 billion to help low and moderate-income households buy homes. $500 million for the infrastructure that supports new housing construction, such as water, sewage, parks and transportation improvements. $450 million to build or renovate an estimated 2,500 units of farmworker housing. $350 million to fund affordable homes for an estimated 1,200 University of California and California State University students. $200 million in housing grants to tribes, which could fund both home construction and renovation. $200 million up for grabs to cities, counties and other groups that pitch pilot projects to develop low-cost housing. How would California pay for it? It would cost the state between $500 million and $600 million each year for about 25 years to repay the cost of the general housing bond, according to the legislative analyst. That money would come from the state’s general fund, and factors in interest. The $1.25 billion for veterans housing would not cost the state anything, as participating vets would pay it off through monthly loan payments. Have we done anything like this before? California voters approved (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2024/03/election-result-proposition-1/) (by the slimmest of margins) another bond (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/03/prop-1-update/) in 2024 that provided $2 billion to fund homes (https://calmatters.org/health/mental-health/2025/06/prop-1-mental-health-awards/) for people who need mental health and addiction services and veterans. That 2024 bond also was dubbed Prop. 1. What do supporters say? Supporters include housing developers and advocates, veterans groups, the California State University and University of California boards, groups representing California’s cities and counties, Democratic legislators and Gov. Gavin Newsom. Donors backing Prop. 1 also reflect some who would benefit. The campaign has received more than $12 million, including about $2 million from carpenters’ unions, $1 million from Airbnb and $1 million from Building a Better California, a PAC funded by Google founder Sergey Brin and other Silicon Valley billionaires. Sign up for free Δ Vivian Wan, chief executive of affordable housing provider Abode, says her organization has four projects with a planned total of about 230 units in the works that she hopes Prop. 1 will fund. Three are in the Bay Area and one is in Yolo County. Without that cash infusion, all four projects are stalled, she said. Projects for homeless and low-income residents need large subsidies since their tenants don’t pay enough in rent to offset the cost of building. They often also have to fund additional services, such as case managers to help residents navigate their physical and mental health, addictions, finances and more. City and county dollars can pay for some but not all of that. Prop. 1 would be “huge,” Wan said. But it wouldn’t magically solve the housing crisis. “Is it enough? Absolutely not,” she said. “We are lightyears behind in terms of production to meet the need. We have underinvested in housing for decades. This is going to help, for sure, but we really need a permanent source.” What do opponents say? When this measure (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260sb417) came up for a floor vote before the Legislature, two Republican senators voted no, as well as seven Republican assemblymembers. Sen. Tony Strickland (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/tony-strickland-188489), a Republican from Huntington Beach who opposed the bill, said calling it “The Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act of 2026” amounted to a bait-and-switch maneuver, as only a small fraction of the total funds go to vets. “It really just says that you’re using veterans to pass your $10 billion general obligation bond,” he said during a June hearing. And, he said, there are better ways to get families into housing than using a bond to “borrow money against the future.” The strong revenues California experienced this year won’t continue, making it risky to push the state deeper into debt, he said. Quick overview: Proposition 1
LAist's AirTalk host Larry Mantle's ballot cram session gets you ready to vote with guests Michael Alvarez, of Caltech, Sara Sadhwani of Pomona College, and Lee E. Ohanian of UCLA and the Hoover Institution.
This measure asks voters to approve $11.25 billion in state bonds for various affordable housing strategies. The revenue would go toward the construction of new income-restricted apartments, supportive housing for tenants overcoming homelessness, mortgage assistance for veterans and a number of other programs.
What’s at stake?
According to recent U.S. Census Bureau statistics (https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R48945), about 54% of California renters officially qualify as “cost-burdened,” meaning they pay more than 30% of their income on rent. The only states with higher levels of rent burden are Florida and Nevada.
California needs to build about 1 million new homes (https://laist.com/news/housing-homelessness/affordable-housing-units-setback-california) specifically for low-income residents, based on current statewide planning goals. Proposition 1 aims to speed up that process by raising money from bonds that would be repaid from the state’s general fund over the next 25 years.
Official title on the ballot: Prop. 1: Authorizes bonds for housing affordability programs
Language you will see (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/index.htm) on the ballot:
Authorizes $11.25 billion in state general obligation bonds for housing affordability programs, including multifamily rental housing, mortgages for veterans, supportive housing, preservation of existing affordable housing, and downpayment assistance. Fiscal Impact : Increased state cost of $500 million to $600 million annually for about 25 years to repay the housing bond.
What your vote means
A "yes" vote means: The state could borrow $11.25 billion to support veterans and affordable housing.
A "no" vote means: The state could not borrow $11.25 billion to support veterans and affordable housing.
Understanding Prop. 1
Affordable housing units generally set rents at no more than 30% of a tenant’s income. That means they often do not generate enough rental income to be profitable for developers. That’s where public subsidies come in.
In recent years, California has put more funding toward creating low-cost housing. According to a recent state legislative analysis (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billAnalysisClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB417), California has funded various affordable housing programs with $8 billion from the state’s general fund since 2019.
But some of those funding streams are now drying up.
A previous measure also called Proposition 1, passed by voters in 2018, approved $4 billion in bonds for affordable housing and veteran mortgage programs. Proposition 2, also from 2018, put $2 billion toward the creation of 7,000 supportive units for formerly unhoused tenants. Both funds are now depleted.
Those state funds have run out at a time when state lawmakers say California can no longer rely on Washington, D.C., to expand or continue federal affordable housing efforts. They argue Prop. 1 could make an immediate difference for an estimated 45,000 units that are in the construction pipeline but have yet to break ground due to a lack of gap financing.
Here’s what supporters say
In addition to helping low-income renters, formerly unhoused tenants and veterans, Proposition 1 proponents say the bond would also fund programs specifically designed to help college students, youth exiting foster care, farmworkers, tribal communities and low-income first-time homebuyers.
Notable endorsements: The coalition (https://yesonprop1ca.com/coalition) of Proposition 1 supporters includes the Southern California Association of Nonprofit Housing, the California Association of Veterans Service Agencies and the California Federation of Labor Unions.
Here’s what opponents say
There is no organized campaign against Proposition 1, but a handful of Republican state lawmakers voted against putting it on the ballot. State Sen. Tony Strickland, who represents coastal Orange County and pockets of L.A. County, said Proposition 1 has a “noble goal” but could end up “bankrupting our next generation.” He said, “We could definitely find $10 billion within the general fund spending, and within our normal budget, without doing bond indebtedness.”
Notable opposition: The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, a frequent critic of new California revenue proposals, opposes Proposition 1 in its election guide (https://www.hjta.org/2026votingguide/). The group writes that bonds rely on borrowed money, and debt service costs add up over time. "When used to pay for programs instead of capital projects, it’s a much greater burden on taxpayers than just paying for these programs from the budget," the Howard Jarvis guide says.
Potential financial impact
The California Legislative Analyst’s Office said (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=1&year=2026) repayment of the Proposition 1 bonds would cost the state between $500 million and $600 million each year for the next 25 years.
Because bonds would need to be repaid with interest, the legislative analysis said costs would likely end up about 15% higher than if the state paid for the programs with existing funding.
In total, the analysis said Proposition 1 would provide subsidies for an estimated 40,000 rental apartments, 2,500 farmworker units, 1,200 college student beds and would help up to 40,000 households achieve homeownership, including about 2,100 veterans.
Watch the ballot cram session analysis
To watch the full ballot cram session, click here (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XfPTVjCzn8E&t=339s).
What it takes to win
A majority is needed to pass.

I'm sorting through how the editorial boards line up on this: the Chronicle, McClatchy papers, the Santa Cruz Sentinel, the Daily Cal, and several advocacy groups are in favor, while the OC Register and its sister papers are against it.

I'm moving on to the rest of the editorial split: the Bay Area News Group, the San Diego Union-Tribune, the Press Democrat, and a few others land on the no side, while the Republican Party, C.A.R., the Greens, and Peace and Freedom take no position. Next I want the full IGS endorsement table and a few key editorials from each side, plus the fiscal numbers behind the debate: the projected structural deficit, the debt service share, and the per-unit cost of affordable housing.

I'm weighing the fiscal side next: the structural deficit, debt service, and what affordable housing costs per unit. I'm also checking the federal tax-credit changes, whether the bond would move housing prices or rents, and whether down payment assistance tends to push prices up.

By U T Editorial Board (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/author/u-t-editorial-board/)
PUBLISHED: September 11, 2026 at 5:40 PM PDT

From 2000 to 2024, according to Ballotpedia (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_2,_Use_Millionaire%27s_Tax_Revenue_for_Homelessness_Prevention_Housing_Bonds_Measure_(2018)), California voters approved eight housing measures. Most of their $17 billion-plus in funding came from state bonds. Some measures focused on adding “affordable housing” in general; some on helping veterans; some on sheltering the homeless. All were billed as obvious, straightforward responses to a chronic housing shortage.
But none laid a glove on the problem. When “affordable” units cost $800,000 or more to build, billions in funding doesn’t add enough housing to matter in a state with 39 million people.
The extreme cost of housing remains the main reason a state whose leaders love to boast about how big its economy is has the highest percentage of impoverished residents (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2025/09/california-living-costs-highest-poverty/) in the nation. The epicenter of American poverty isn’t a grim, jobs-starved metro area in the Deep South or Appalachia, it’s Los Angeles County (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2025/09/california-living-costs-highest-poverty/).
So why do state politicians keep asking voters to approve costly, ineffective initiatives? Because the “Message: I care” optics of such measures allow these pols to insist they actually care about California’s extreme cost of living.
Which brings us to Proposition 1 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_1,_Veteran_and_Housing_Assistance_Programs_Bond_Measure_(2026)), placed on the November ballot by the Legislature. It would let the state borrow $11.25 billion to build “affordable” housing that is only affordable to the relative handful of residents lucky enough to get a taxpayer-subsidized unit. With broad institutional support, little opposition and a smart campaign that focuses on how the measure prioritizes helping veterans, it seems sure to pass.
But the U-T Editorial Board opposes costly propositions — whose bonds must be paid off for decades to come — if their primary effect is to create an illusion of progress. As progressive reformers Ezra Klein and Derek Thompson pointed out (https://www.noahpinion.blog/p/book-review-abundance) in “Abundance,” their persuasive 2025 book, many influential California Democrats value process over results. They see signaling their shared values to party voters as more important than their performance in office.
This is particularly unfortunate because if voters this November approve Proposition 45 (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/2026/09/11/endorsement-yes-on-prop-45-to-reform-ceqa-limit-state-dysfunction/) — reducing the tools in CEQA that have been used for 50-plus years to block housing construction — state lawmakers would have a real opportunity to create change. According to Princeton economist Evan Soltas’ review (https://x.com/esoltas/status/2098162675989565925/photo/1) of 60 large U.S. cities, it takes longer or nearly as long to get a single-family home building permit in San Francisco, Los Angeles or San Diego as it does to permit and build such a home in Indianapolis, Fort Worth or Colorado Springs. The time it takes to get a permit and to build a home directly correlates with its final cost.
To fix the housing mess, CEQA reforms should only be the start.
Reducing the state’s hostility to non-union construction companies would help.
So would new thinking about zoning that frees up hundreds of square miles of agricultural parcels for housing.
So would embracing the sturdy new versions of inexpensive prefabricated homes that have been very popular in Japan (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/09/condo-construction-bill-dies/) and Great Britain (https://www.theguardian.com/business/2023/apr/14/fast-build-modular-homes-an-answer-to-the-uk-housing-crisis).
So would passage of a bill that would fix flawed regulations that have the effect of incentivizing lawsuits against condo builders; such a measure (Assembly Bill 1903) died in the Capitol two weeks ago without ever drawing a single “no” vote (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/09/condo-construction-bill-dies/) in the Assembly or Senate.
This specific and constructive agenda could make a real difference. But for a dozen years, lawmakers have preferred posturing about the housing status quo to meaningfully addressing it.
Proposition 1 is one more example.

Endorsement: Affordable housing in California isn’t going to pay for itself. Is Prop 1 the answer?
Proposition 1 would authorize California to issue $11.25 billion in new bonds to create and preserve affordable housing and expand opportunities for owning a home.
S.F. Chronicle illustration from Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Sep 26, 2026
The housing debate in California often feels a bit like fighting with your rambling uncle during Thanksgiving dinner. But there’s generally one island of universal agreement in a sea of rage: the need for more affordable housing.
A recent legislative analysis found (https://ahcd.assembly.ca.gov/system/files/2026-04/ahcd-hearing-packet-for-the-website.pdf) that 2.2 million extremely low-income and low-income California households are competing for just 664,000 affordable rental homes. To even come close to meeting demand, the California Department of Housing and Community Development estimated the state needs at least 1 million new affordable units by 2031, (https://www.hcd.ca.gov/sites/default/files/docs/policy-and-research/plan-report/StateofCADraft-2022-2023-AAP-12-6-22.pdf) including about 47,000 in San Francisco (https://sfgov.legistar.com/View.ashx?GUID=EDE50759-96D2-4873-846C-70851EEE4957&ID=15560084&M=F&).
Building this level of subsidized affordable housing will be neither easy nor cheap — and there’s lots of competition for limited funds.
In 2018, voters approved $4 billion in bonds for affordable and veteran housing (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=1&year=2018), all of which was allocated by the end of 2023. California’s Multifamily Housing Program (https://www.hcd.ca.gov/funding/mhp) — the state’s primary vehicle for providing developers with low-cost loans to build, rehabilitate and preserve affordable housing — has $9 in requests for every dollar available, a California Budget and Policy Center analysis found (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/proposition-1-californias-veterans-and-affordable-housing-bond/).
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Endorsement : Who should replace Nancy Pelosi in Congress? It’s not even a choice (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/scott-wiener-connie-chan-pelosi-22448323.php)
Proposition 1 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop1-text-proposed-laws.pdf), which the state Legislature placed on the November ballot with bipartisan support (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billVotesClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB417), would authorize California to issue $11.25 billion in new bonds to create and preserve affordable housing and expand homeownership opportunities. Befitting the broad consensus on the state’s affordability crisis, it has no formal opposition.
The measure is rigidly prescriptive in its allocation of funds.
It allocates $7.2 billion to the Multifamily Housing Program — which the measure’s author, Assembly Member Buffy Wicks, D-Oakland, described in an endorsement interview as the “workhorse” of California’s efforts to develop affordable rental homes. Of that pool, $1.15 billion would be reserved for supportive housing and services for people at risk of or exiting homelessness, with $150 million set aside for youth who are homeless or in foster care. Another $750 million would go to renovating and modernizing existing affordable housing.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Outside of that bucket, $1.25 billion is earmarked for the CalVet Home Loan program (https://www.calvet.ca.gov/HomeLoans), which uses the proceeds from bond sales to provide loans to veterans to purchase homes. This program doesn’t cost taxpayers anything because veterans repay the cost of the bonds and interest through their loan payments. (Some Republican lawmakers accused Democrats of trying to inflate voter support for the measure by calling it the Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond when only about 10% of the overall funds go to veterans.)
Another $600 million would go to local agencies and nonprofits — such as Habitat for Humanity — to work with would-be homeowners to build or finance affordable homes, while $500 million would go to down-payment assistance for eligible first-time home buyers.
Among the measure’s other earmarks: $500 million for developing infrastructure — such as water and sewage lines — to support affordable housing, $450 million to build and rehabilitate farmworker housing, $350 million to be split evenly between the University of California and California State University systems for student housing, $200 million to tribal housing programs and $200 million to local grants and pilot programs that “demonstrate innovative, cost-saving approaches to creating or preserving affordable housing.”
If this seems like a dizzying array of priorities, that’s because it is.

Rick M
Walnut Creek, CA
10/02/26
0
Your endorsement of Scott Wiener deserves a closer examination of the philosophy behind his housing and wealth policies.
Unequal wealth is a fact; it does not, by itself, establish an injustice or a government duty to reduce it. People build wealth through work, saving, investment, entrepreneurship, risk and circumstance. Wiener’s policies reflect a different premise: that disparities in wealth and access to affluent communities are problems government should correct through taxation and housing policy. His housing policies use state authority to require communities—including affluent, low-density communities—to accommodate housing across income levels, with consequences for noncompliance. This shifts important land-use decisions from local communities to the state.Meanwhile, many Californians earn too much for substantial assistance but too little to buy homes in expensive communities. Policy should focus on upward mobility—better schools, safer communities, etc. - not simply equal $$
Prop 1 is the product of years of legislative sausage-making: It combines bits and pieces of policies proposed by lawmakers and advocates, each with a specific group or issue they’re trying to address.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
So, is the measure too unwieldy — and divided among too many different groups and interests — to be effective?
Wicks told us she is “very aware of that concern” but emphasized that each of the programs receiving funding in the bond is “a proven model that we know works.”
Altogether, Prop 1 could subsidize the creation of as many as 40,000 affordable rental units, plus 2,500 for farmworkers and another 1,200 for college students, according to estimates from the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop1-110326.pdf) — while helping 40,000 households, including 2,100 veterans, achieve homeownership. (A separate November ballot measure, Prop 37 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-37-housing-home-loans-22422795.php), would provide down-payment assistance to middle-income Californians, at no cost to taxpayers.)
This, of course, is a drop in the bucket of California’s housing needs — at a not insignificant cost. The state will need to make estimated annual payments of $500 million to $600 million from the general fund for 25 years to pay off the bond — 15% more expensive than an upfront payment. This will also reduce the money available for other critical programs at a time when California faces years of projected future budget deficits (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/5101).
But there is good reason to believe that California will, as Wicks put it, “have a better ROI on these resources today” than in the past.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
That’s because the state has in recent years significantly reduced the roadblocks that delay housing and drive up the cost of production — including by exempting all infill development from unnecessary review (https://www.sfchronicle.com/california/article/ceqa-housing-roadblocks-newsom-20402835.php) under the California Environmental Quality Act and streamlining dense housing near transit (https://www.sfchronicle.com/bayarea/article/housing-transit-map-yimby-21075831.php).
Ongoing efforts to streamline the state’s maze of affordable housing financing programs (https://lao.ca.gov/publications/report/5199) into one consolidated application (https://ahcd.assembly.ca.gov/system/files/2026-08/ab-519-july-2026-deliverable-7.1.26-final-afforable-housing-finance-workgroup.pdf), along with other reforms, could also slash development costs by $60,000 to $70,000 per unit (https://www.hcd.ca.gov/about-hcd/newsroom/more-housing-faster-governor-newsom-signs-historic-housing-affordability-reforms).
“We’re at a great moment in time to actually have the best impact on housing that I’ve seen in my career,” Ray Pearl, executive director of the California Housing Consortium, told us.
One thing the measure doesn’t fully account for: upkeep. As the Chronicle has rigorously documented (https://www.sfchronicle.com/projects/2022/san-francisco-sros/), many deed-restricted affordable homes in places like San Francisco are deteriorating. (https://www.sfchronicle.com/sf/article/affordable-housing-sale-21251741.php) Prop 1 only sets aside a relative pittance for rehabilitation.
This is a fundamental problem with California’s focus on 100% affordable housing developments — rents don’t cover the bills, necessitating significant ongoing subsidies.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Legislators would be wise to pursue other paths, such as Washington state’s tax incentives (https://www.theurbanist.org/state-senate-greenlights-sweeping-tod-housing-bill/) to build affordable units inside market-rate developments, to share the burden of upkeep with the private sector.
Wicks told us California also needs to restructure its budgets to establish “sustained ongoing funding for affordable housing so that we’re not having to have this bond conversation every six years.”

We agree.
In the interim, however, the need for more affordable housing is too desperate to wait. Prop 1 is well-positioned to reap the benefits of the state’s new streamlining laws. We recommend a yes vote.

The problem underlying California’s housing crisis comes down to this: the cost of construction.
It constrains new supply. And the only way to recoup the costs of what does get built requires high rents and mortgages or — in the case of affordable housing — public subsidies.
Unfortunately, the solution to this crisis offered by two statewide propositions has nothing to do with addressing prohibitive building costs. Instead, their answer is to load Californians with debt while delivering bonanzas to home developers and builders.

Proposition 1 leaves taxpayers indebted; Proposition 37, homebuyers.
Reject both.
Proposition 1
This measure, placed on the ballot by the state Legislature through Senate Bill 407, is an expensive pandering potpourri of giveaways. Veterans, farmworkers, students, tribes are all the ostensible beneficiaries.
Here’s how it is supposed to work:
Proposition 1 would authorize the state to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds, all earmarked for various housing programs. The bulk of the bonds, $7.2 billion, would be spent acquiring, building or renovating apartments. The backers of this proposition optimistically estimate that it would subsidize the construction of “up to” 40,000 multifamily rental units as well as 2,500 housing units for farmworkers and 1,200 beds for university students.
Another $1.1 billion would provide homeownership assistance for 40,000 families. The remainder of funds would go toward infrastructure projects ($500 million), farmworker housing ($450 million), student housing at the UC and Cal State systems ($350 million), and tribal housing ($200 million).
Additionally, $1.25 billion would be dedicated to home loan assistance for veterans. (This program is not expected to create direct costs as participating veterans would pay monthly payments to the state, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office.)
The need for affordable housing and housing assistance in this state is undeniable. More than two in five households spend, at least, 30% of their incomes on housing.
However, Proposition 1 would only provide a drop in the bucket towards adding to the state’s housing supply, all while hamstringing state spending and burdening taxpayers with decades of debt. The LAO projects that paying off $10 billion in bond debt incurred by this measure would require annual payments between $500 million to $600 million for a quarter of a century. These payments would come from California’s checking account, the General Fund. Because the state has to pay interest on the money it borrows, per the LAO, the total cost of the bond would be about 15% more (after adjusting for inflation) than if the state paid up front with money it already has.
Perhaps that would be acceptable if this burst of spending would make a long-term difference, but it’s doubtful.
Consider that California needs to build 2.5 million new homes, including 1 million affordable ones, to keep up with demand.
But this measure would add only 4% toward the affordable total, and that’s only under pie-in-the-sky circumstances.
More disconcerting is how this measure would do nothing to attack the root of the affordable housing cost problem:
Building subsidized housing in California costs 1.5 times the average cost of building already-exorbitant market-rate housing here, according to a 2025 RAND study.
The nonpartisan think tank identified two major reasons for the discrepancy: Local governments charge “unusually large” architectural and engineering fees, and they require that affordable housing developers pay “substantially above-market” wages.
While $200 million of Proposition 1 would go toward “pilot” programs aimed at developing reduced housing models, at least $10 billion would be spent keeping this bloated model afloat.
Proposition 37
This measure looks great on the surface. It would help Californians buy new homes, all without costing taxpayers a dime.
Well, all that glitters isn’t gold.
Proposition 37 would authorize up to $25 billion in revenue bonds for downpayment assistance on newly constructed homes. Eligible buyers could borrow up to 17% of a home’s purchase price through a fixed-rate second mortgage, making a down payment as low as 3%.
For example, consider an $800,000 home. A buyer could put down $24,000, borrow $136,000 through Proposition 37 and then finance the remaining $640,000 using a conventional mortgage.
A 30-year loan at today’s rates would make the monthly costs of that second mortgage more than $900.
Proposition 37 is not reducing the burden of home prices in California.
It’s not solving the affordability crisis.
It’s just a creative way to help Californians take on more debt.
What rightly worries critics is the terms of these additional loans. When borrowers default, the primary mortgage lender gets repaid first, meaning that the owner of the secondary takes on more risk. That would almost certainly mean that investors would require that buyers pay higher rates on their second mortgages than they pay on the first.
The LAO identifies these financing terms and investor participation as significant uncertainties.
Proposition 37 does nothing to address the main obstacle to homeownership in the state: the monthly cost of a conventional mortgage.
While the majority of renters in the state have incomes that would make them eligible to benefit from the measure’s secondary mortgage program, many wouldn’t qualify for a conventional mortgage in the first place even with its down payment assistance, according to the Public Policy Institute of California.
Far from solving the problem of high home prices, Proposition 37 could compound it.
While the measure restricts using the downpayment assistance to previously unpurchased homes, that does not mean that Proposition 37 will unleash a large new supply of housing.
What’s infinitely more probable is that Proposition 37 would expand purchasing power faster than it would induce new construction — and therefore push up prices.

By McClatchy Media’s California editorial board
Updated September 30, 2026 2:22 PM
A drone view of Mirasol Village on Monday, Aug. 3, 2026. Proposition 1 looks to increase homebuilding in California through an $11.25 billion bond measure.
HECTOR AMEZCUA
hamezcua@sacbee.com
California has spent years creating laws that make it easier to build housing. Now it needs to help finance affordable housing (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=1&year=2026&utm_source=chatgpt.com) waiting to be produced at rents many Californians can afford.
There are nearly 40,000 affordable rental homes in the development pipeline (https://www.housingfinance.com/data-trends/california-pipeline-holds-nearly-40000-affordable-homes-seeking-funds) — designed and approved but awaiting sufficient financing to begin construction, according to Enterprise Community Partners, (https://www.enterprisecommunity.org/about) a national housing nonprofit. Proposition 1 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317117857.html) could help close those financing gaps.
THE BEE’S VOTER GUIDE: Your guide to Proposition 1 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317117857.html)
A “yes” vote on Proposition 1 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_1,_Veteran_and_Housing_Assistance_Programs_Bond_Measure_(2026)) would authorize $11.25 billion in bonds: $10 billion for affordable housing and $1.25 billion for a longstandingCalVet home-loan program. (https://veteran.com/start/?src=adw&adg=185122315662&cmp=compterms&desc=calculator&matchtype=p&adid=803809597618&targetid=kwd-297340664879&label=&campaignid=23211217847&extid=&gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=23211217847&gbraid=0AAAAAqq9dHmkha--aWxuqkJFb13gc3lv2&gclid=CjwKCAjwq8PVBhAKEiwA2i3SHZePD1ETl_2tqMBf65xQCzjoSQ7GCNQ3Jj7lr4UZqy9t2I0slreQtBoCALsQAvD_BwE) Funds raised by Prop. 1 would support construction and preservation of affordable apartments (https://www.enterprisecommunity.org/learning-center/resources/2026-california-affordable-housing-production-pipeline?utm_source=chatgpt.com), supportive housing, homeownership assistance, farmworker and tribal housing, student housing and infrastructure needed for affordable developments.
It’s undeniable that Californians struggle with rents they cannot afford, homelessness and home prices that put ownership beyond the reach of many working families.
Private developers generally cannot build housing for low-income and extremely low-income households and charge rents these families can afford while recovering the cost of construction. Every dollar the state invests leverages $4 from federal, local and private funding, according to the California Budget & Policy Center.
And taxpayers wouldn’t be purchasing a fleeting benefit. Affordable apartments receiving these subsidies generally must remain affordable for 55 years. Proponents estimate that turnover during that period could allow roughly 500,000 households to benefit.
There is a cost. TheLegislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/) estimates that repaying the $10 billion housing bond will cost the state’s General Fund $500 million to $600 million annually for about 25 years — roughly one-quarter of 1% of today’s General Fund budget. The separate $1.25 billion veterans portion is expected to be repaid through veterans’ mortgage payments, as previous CalVet bonds have been.
Opponents rightly say that housing in California is too expensive to build. But their argument that lawmakers should attack those costs instead of subsidizing affordable housing presents a false choice.
California can do both.
In just the past two legislative sessions, for instance, lawmakers have approved a series of changes to speed up environmental reviews and permitting, reduce some impact fees and simplify affordable-housing financing. The state’s newOne-Stop Shop financing reforms (https://ternercenter.berkeley.edu/research-and-policy/california-governors-budget-proposal-advances-a-one-stop-shop-for-affordable-housing/) and impact-fee changes alone are estimated by the Newsom administration to reduce affordable housing costs by $60,000-$70,000 per unit.
Government should eliminate unnecessary expenses, but it cannot eliminate the real costs of roads, schools, water, sewer and other infrastructure communities need as they grow. Nor is government responsible for every rising construction expense. Land, materials, interest rates, insurance, labor, contractor practices and other factors all contribute.
That’s why Proposition 1 should become something more than another infusion of money. California should use this enormous investment to learn precisely why affordable housing costs what it does.
For every project receiving bond money, the state should collect standardized information about land, construction, financing, permit and impact fees, professional services, labor expense, financing sources, approval times and change orders. This would allow researchers to compare similar projects being financed and determine why one costs $450,000 per unit while another costs $800,000 a unit.
And Californians should not have to become government accounting detectives to find the results.
The state should create a simple, prominently displayed public dashboard showing money awarded and spent, units produced and preserved, project locations, costs per unit and completion times. Proponents agreed with us that such transparency is achievable.
That need became obvious when we asked them what measurable results from California’s 2018 housing bond justify returning to voters for substantially more money. They cited strong demand and the fact that its funding was fully committed within five years, but could not readily provide the kind of statewide performance measures voters deserve.
Housing is fundamental to economic mobility. A family struggling to keep a roof over its head has little opportunity to save, educate its children, emphasize wellness or build financial security.
California needs those homes. It also needs to learn how to build the next ones faster and for less.
Proposition 1 gives California (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/proposition-1-californias-veterans-and-affordable-housing-bond/) the opportunity to do better.

Report
Proposition 1: California’s Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond
A $11.25 Billion Bond to Continue Building Affordable Homes for Californians
July 2026 | By Monica Davalos (https://calbudgetcenter.org/people/monica-davalos/)
Print Report
key takeaway
Proposition 1, appearing on the November 2026 ballot, would provide funding for affordable housing and accessible homeownership. Prop. 1 asks voters to authorize a $11.25 billion general obligation bond to fund programs that support the creation and preservation of affordable housing, expand homebuying opportunities for low- and moderate-income Californians and veterans, and invest in permanent solutions to solve homelessness. If Prop. 1 is approved, it would replenish funding for several successful state programs that have exhausted their resources. Prop. 1 was placed on the ballot by the Legislature through passage of Senate Bill 417 (2026) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB417).
table of contents
How Has California Expanded Affordable Housing & What Gaps Remain?
Why Is Affordable Housing Funding Running Out & How Would Prop. 1 Help?
What Affordable Housing and Homeownership Programs Would Prop. 1 Fund?
What Benefits Would Prop. 1 Create for California’s Economy & Communities?
How Would Prop. 1 Be Repaid?
Prop. 1 and Prop. 38 Draw From Same Bonding Capacity, Face Important Trade Offs
Prop. 1 Supporters and Opponents
How Has California Expanded Affordable Housing & What Gaps Remain?
Over the past six years, California has nearly tripled (https://calhousingpartnership.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/CHP_2026-Housing-Needs-Report-FINAL.pdf) the number of new affordable homes it funds. Yet the state continues to face a severe shortage of affordable housing, particularly for Californians with the lowest incomes. California needs more than 2.5 million new homes, including at least 1 million homes that are affordable to lower-income households. Housing cost pressures fall hardest on California renters as nearly half pay unaffordable rents — a hardship that disproportionately impacts Black and Latinx renters with low incomes, older adults, mixed-status families, and people with disabilities.
Unlike market-rate or luxury housing, affordable housing projects typically cannot be built without subsidies because affordable rents do not generate enough revenue to cover development or operating costs. As a result, affordable housing projects rely on multiple funding streams to close financing gaps. Currently, more than 46,000 affordable homes across California (491 developments) (https://www.enterprisecommunity.org/sites/default/files/2024-04/State_Pipeline_2024_FINAL.pdf) are waiting for the last bit of state funding needed to break ground. Prop. 1 would provide funding for various programs that help bridge the financial gap to keep affordable housing construction moving.
Why Is Affordable Housing Funding Running Out & How Would Prop. 1 Help?
Despite the ongoing housing affordability challenges Californians are facing, state funding for affordable housing has largely disappeared. Over the past several years, affordable housing programs have relied on one-time General Fund investments (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/protecting-progress-state-housing-and-homelessness-funding-must-continue/) to supplement voter-approved housing bonds, but those investments have drastically declined. The 2026 Budget Act only includes one-time investments in two significant affordable housing programs: $500 million for state Low Income Housing Tax Credits and $200 million for the Multifamily Housing Program, effectively leaving multiple programs (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/first-look-understanding-the-governors-proposed-2026-27-california-budget/#h-proposed-budget-includes-no-new-state-funding-for-affordable-housing) without additional funds. Beyond these investments, there is no meaningful ongoing or one-time investment from the state General Fund for affordable housing development.
The state’s remaining modest affordable housing funding sources, including the Affordable Housing and Sustainable Communities Program (AHSC), funded through Cap-and-Invest; state and federal Low-Income Housing Tax Credits; and SB 2 planning funds are insufficient to meet the demand and often require additional funding to be fully leveraged. The AHSC program was expected to receive nearly $800 million per year for affordable housing, but recent changes by the California Air Resources Board put that funding at risk.
Curious About Other Ballot Propositions?
Browse our collection of resources covering California’s statewide ballot measures to help you understand what’s at stake for California this November.
See More Resources (https://calbudgetcenter.org/issues/ballot-propositions/)
The funding approved by voters through the 2018 Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act has been fully committed — exhausted within five years, by the end of 2023, due to overwhelming demand. The state’s flagship Multifamily Housing Program, which relied on funding from the bond and one-time General Fund investments, is routinely oversubscribed by roughly 9 to 1. Together these signal that the barrier to building more affordable housing in California isn’t a lack of will or projects — it’s a lack of sustainable funding.
Without new state investments, affordable housing production will stall just as California is making meaningful progress and as federal cuts threaten to make it even more difficult for Californians to make ends meet, which is why state lawmakers placed Prop. 1 on the ballot.
What Affordable Housing and Homeownership Programs Would Prop. 1 Fund?
Prop. 1 asks voters to authorize $11.25 billion in general obligation (GO) bonds that would support the construction and preservation of affordable rental homes, expand homeownership assistance for low- and moderate-income homebuyers, including veterans, and provide permanent housing for people at risk of or experiencing homelessness. Within these categories, it would provide some funding for programs that serve distinct populations, such as California tribes, farmworkers, unhoused youth, and college students. The bond funds would be allocated as follows:
Affordable Housing Development and Preservation
$5.1 billion for the Multifamily Housing Program (MHP) , which supports the construction, rehabilitation, or preservation of affordable rental housing. At least 10% of units in a MHP development must be available for extremely low-income households who are at the highest risk of facing homelessness. This is one of California’s model affordable housing development programs.
$1.15 billion for supportive housing through the MHP program. Supportive housing provides stable homes with wrap-around services for people who were chronically homeless or at risk of becoming so. These funds can be used for operating subsidy reserves, which are critical to the longevity and sustainability of permanent supportive housing.
Up to 15% — $150 million — would be allocated as grants to acquire or build permanent supportive housing among other specified uses.
Another $150 million is carved out for the capital development or acquisition of youth housing through MHP. This would serve current or former foster youth, homeless minors or youth, or youth at risk of homelessness.
$750 million for the Portfolio Reinvestment Program, which provides funding to rehabilitate and extend the long-term affordability of state-funded rental multifamily housing projects that are at risk of conversion to market-rate housing.
$500 million for the Infill Infrastructure Grant Program . This would provide incentive grants to assist with new construction and rehabilitation of infrastructure that supports high-density affordable and mixed-income housing in locations designated as infill.
$450 million for the Joe Serna, Jr. Farmworker Housing Program to fund grants or loans for the construction or rehabilitation of housing for agricultural employees and their families.
$350 million for affordable student housing projects to be split evenly between the University of California and the California State University.
$200 million for a new Community Anti-Displacement and Preservation Program, which helps protect unsubsidized housing that may naturally be affordable and requires long-term affordability regulations.
$200 million for the Tribal Housing Grant Program which finances housing and housing-related activities to enable tribes to rebuild and reconstitute their communities.
$200 million to the Affordable Housing Innovation Fund for the Local Housing Trust Fund Matching Grant Program. This would fund competitive grants or loans to local housing trust funds that develop, own, lend, or invest in affordable housing and would be used to create pilot programs to demonstrate innovative approaches to creating or preserving affordable housing.
Homeownership
$1.25 billion for the CalVet Home Loan Program (https://www.calvet.ca.gov/HomeLoans) to help veterans and their families purchase homes. This portion of the bond would be repaid through mortgage (principal and interest) payments.
$600 million for the CalHome program. CalHome provides forgivable loans for lower-income households in self-help homeownership projects, including subdivisions and manufactured homes.
$500 million for the My Home downpayment assistance program to fund low-to-moderate income home purchase assistance programs.
What Benefits Would Prop. 1 Create for California’s Economy & Communities?
Prop. 1 would help expand and preserve California’s affordable housing supply while generating economic benefits and advancing the state’s housing goals. The bond would help close the financing gap for affordable rental homes, which serve lower-income California families and include seniors, people with disabilities, farmworkers, college students, and unhoused youth. According to legislative analyses (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB417), the bond is expected to:
Produce more than 40,000 new affordable homes for lower-income families and individuals.
Preserve more than 5,500 existing affordable homes , ensuring they remain affordable for future generations.
Create more than 53,000 construction jobs through building new housing across the state.
Generate $1.3 billion in state and local tax revenue that supports local communities and public services.
Every $1 invested in state affordable housing leverages roughly $4 (https://roadmaphome.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/Roadmap-Home-Report-2026.pdf) in federal, local, and private investment, maximizing the impact of public dollars. Affordable housing also delivers economic, health, and environmental benefits (https://affordablehomes.calhousingpartnership.org/). For example:
Children who grow up in affordable housing earn a median of $51,000 more over their lifetimes,
Permanent supportive housing saves an estimated $1.80 in public costs for every $1 invested (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8863642/pdf/nihms-1768403.pdf), and
Building homes near jobs and transit lowers transportation costs while reducing greenhouse gas emissions (https://www.hcd.ca.gov/policy-and-research/intersectional-policy-work/housing-and-climate-change).
Together, these investments would expand housing opportunities, reduce housing instability, strengthen local economies, and help California meet its long-term housing needs.
How Would Prop. 1 Be Repaid?
Prop. 1 asks voters to authorize a total of $11.25 billion in GO bonds, divided as follows:
A $10 billion GO bond for affordable housing and homeownership programs that would be repaid from the state’s General Fund, and
A $1.25 billion veterans’ bond, a type of tax-exempt GO bond, for the CalVet Home Loan program that would be repaid through mortgage payments, with the General Fund as a backstop.
California voters often pass GO bonds to fund infrastructure projects that are designed to serve the public over many generations, as has been the case with affordable housing. Voters have also historically passed veterans’ bonds for CalVet to support homeownership opportunities for veterans.
GO bonds are repaid from the state’s General Fund. Repaying the $10 billion bond would cost $580 million per year for the next 30 years, for a total estimated cost of $17.4 billion ($10 billion in principal and $7.39 billion in interest). As of the governor’s proposed 2026-27 budget, California had $6.3 billion in General Fund debt service for GO bonds, or roughly 2.6% of General Fund expenditures.
In contrast, veterans bonds are generally self-supporting because they are repaid through principal and interest payments made by CalVet Home Loan Program borrowers. However, they are still GO bonds and are ultimately backed by the state’s General Fund. If program revenues were insufficient to cover the debt service, the General Fund would be responsible for the difference. It is unclear how often, if ever, the General Fund has had to backfill debt payments for previous veterans bonds.
Prop. 1 bond dollars would replenish depleted affordable housing programs. But bond dollars alone will not solve the housing shortage, nor would they replace the need for ongoing investments to meet the state’s substantial housing needs.
Prop. 1 and Prop. 38 Draw From Same Bonding Capacity, Face Important Trade Offs
Voters face two GO bond measures on the November 2026 ballot: Prop. 1 and Proposition 38. Prop. 38 would authorize $8.4 billion in GO bonds to support research and development in immunology and immunotherapy. Voters should weigh how each proposal addresses the state’s most pressing needs, fits within California’s limited borrowing capacity, and affects the state’s ability to invest in services that help families today and in the future.
Like all GO bonds, Prop. 38 would require long-term General Fund debt-service payments — estimated at $500 million annually (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Initiative/2025-026) for 25 years — reducing budget and bonding capacity for other state priorities. If both Prop. 1 and Prop. 38 are approved, it would reduce General Fund dollars by roughly $1.1 billion annually.
Public sector investment in scientific research is needed, particularly given federal cuts, but Prop. 38 raises important fiscal and policy considerations. GO bonds are conventionally used to finance infrastructure projects — like roads, bridges, or housing — that can be used over decades, roughly matching the time it takes to repay the bond itself.
Funding research through GO bonds does not work the same way. Bond-funded research gets most of the dollars upfront for grants, salaries, and operating costs, but are not guaranteed to be built into a lasting asset. Research findings do compound overtime, but the bond dollars themselves are depleted after a few years. The state then spends years or decades paying interest on bonds that stopped directly funding work long ago. So while scientific research needs funding, a GO bond is not the appropriate funding mechanism. Plus, half of Prop. 38’s funding would be concentrated on a limited set of health conditions, even though California already has multiple public and private research institutions (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Initiative/2025-026) conducting work in these areas.
Prop. 1 doesn’t confront these same challenges. While previous affordable housing bond dollars were also used up quickly, they left behind affordable homes that will continue to serve numerous families for decades. Affordable housing developments that use state dollars must have affordability requirements for at least 55 years — way beyond the repayment of the bonds with which they’re financed. The community benefits and capital assets outlast the debt, which is the intended purpose of GO bonds.
Prop. 1 Supporters and Opponents
Prop. 1 is supported by a broad coalition (https://www.housingbondca.com/coalition) of organizations representing housing, business, labor, local government, older adults, tenants, homelessness, urban planning, construction, environmental, and civil rights interests, among others.
Official opposition has been limited. The primary opponents on record include a few Republican state legislators who voted against (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billVotesClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB417) placing the measure on the ballot.
The California Budget & Policy Center is a nonpartisan research and analysis nonprofit and does not endorse or oppose ballot measures. This analysis reflects the institutional position of the Budget Center, developed and reviewed by our policy leadership team.

Housing & Homelessness (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/?issue=housing-homelessness)

What Would Proposition 42 Mean for California?
Prop. 42 would prohibit new taxes on the ownership of certain assets as well as taxes that apply retroactively. # Your last-minute guide to all California propositions
## Proposition 1
Proposition 1 asks voters to let the state borrow $11.25 billion through the sale of bonds to build and maintain housing that low- and middle-income residents can afford.

In this post, we summarize state bonds, the state’s current debt levels, and its annual debt service payments.
# Background on Bonds
These are:
- ***General Obligation (GO) Bonds.*** GO bonds must be approved by the voters and their repayment is guaranteed by the state’s general taxing power.
Most of these are directly paid off from the state’s General Fund, which is largely supported by tax revenues.
Some, however, are paid for by other revenue sources, with the General Fund only providing back-up support in the event the revenues fall short.

# Overview of State Debt
***How Much Debt Does California Currently Have?*** As shown in Figure 1, California has a total of about $79 billion in outstanding bond debt—the vast majority of which is from GO bonds.
In addition, the Legislature and voters have authorized another $30 billion in bonds that have not yet been issued (sold).
As these bonds get issued in future years, they will increase the state’s outstanding debt.
On the other hand, the debt that is currently outstanding will slowly get paid off, thereby reducing debt in future years.
Over the last decade, outstanding debt has been paid off at roughly the same rate as new debt has been issued, resulting in a relatively steady level of state debt (not adjusting for inflation).

November 3, 2026 Ballot
Page 1 of 2
OVERVIEW OF STATE BOND DEBT
This section describes the state’s bond debt. It also discusses how the bond measures on the
ballot, if approved by voters, would affect state costs to repay bonds.
State Bonds and Their Costs
What Are Bonds? Bonds are a way that governments borrow money. The state government
uses bonds primarily to pay for infrastructure projects that have a long useful life, such as
bridges, dams, prisons, parks, schools, and office buildings. The state sells bonds to investors to
receive up-front funding for these projects and then must repay the investors over a period of
time, typically a couple of decades. This is very similar to the way a family pays off a mortgage
on their home.
What Are the Costs of Bond Financing? The state’s total cost for a project is more if it pays
with bonds than if it pays up front with money it already has. This is because it has to pay
interest on the bonds. The amount of additional cost depends on the interest rate and how long it
takes to repay the bonds. For example, if the state uses a 30-year bond with a 4 percent interest
rate to pay for a project, the total cost is about 15 percent more (after adjusting for inflation) than
if the state paid up front with money it already has.
Most Bonds Must Be Approved by Voters. The State Constitution requires that most new
bonds be approved by voters. These bonds usually are repaid from the state General Fund. (The
General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services, including education,
health care, and prisons.)
Bonds and State Spending
Current Amount of Bond Debt. The state currently is repaying about $80 billion of bonds
from the state General Fund. In addition, the voters and the Legislature previously have approved
about $40 billion of General Fund-supported bonds that have not yet been sold. Most of these
bonds are expected to be sold in the next several years. The state currently is paying about
$6 billion each year from the General Fund to repay bonds. The state will continue to pay a
similar amount over the next few years. This is about 3 percent of the state’s annual General
Fund revenue, which is lower than the historical average of about 4 percent.
This Election’s Impact on Debt Payments. There are two General Fund-supported bond
measures on this ballot: Proposition 1 and Proposition 38. Proposition 1 would allow the state to
borrow $10 billion for affordable housing programs. The cost to repay this bond would be about
$500 million to $600 million each year for 25 years. Proposition 38 would allow the state to
borrow $8.4 billion for immunology and immunotherapy research. The cost to repay this bond
would be about $500 million to $600 million each year for 20 years. The cost to repay both
November 3, 2026 Ballot
Page 2 of 2
bonds would total about $1 billion each year, which is about one-half of 1 percent (0.5 percent)
of the state’s annual General Fund revenue.

2026 California Prop 1 guide: Affordable rentals get $7.2 billion of the $11.25 billion housing bond
Prop 1’s supporters stress “no new taxes,” which is true. The General Fund would still repay $10 billion at $500 million to $600 million a year for about 25 years. Here is what that money buys, and why the $1.25 billion veterans’ share costs the state nothing directly.

California's Proposition 1 is asking voters to borrow $11.25 billion for affordable rental housing, homebuyers and veterans' home loans.
Proposition 1 would let California borrow $11.25 billion by selling general obligation bonds. Ten billion dollars would go to 11 existing state housing programs and be repaid from the General Fund, mostly to build and preserve apartments rented to low-income households, with the rest for homebuyer help, infrastructure, and farmworker, student and tribal housing. The other $1.25 billion would fund CalVet home loans, which veterans repay through their mortgage payments. The Legislative Analyst's Office puts the cost at $500 million to $600 million a year for about 25 years, roughly a quarter of 1% of the General Fund, and estimates the money would subsidize up to 40,000 rental units and help up to 40,000 households with homeownership. The measure creates no new tax; the debt is paid from the state's existing revenue.
The Affordable Housing Bond under Proposition 1 is sending $7.2 billion of its $11.25 billion to rental housing, led by $5.1 billion for the Multifamily Housing Program. Prop 1, the Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act of 2026, is a legislative statute (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/) placed on the ballot by SB 417, which the Legislature passed and Governor Gavin Newsom signed on June 25. It is one of 14 measures in this year's guide (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/) and the third California measure numbered Proposition 1 to borrow for housing since 2018, following the $4 billion veterans and affordable housing bond of 2018 and the $6.38 billion behavioral health bond voters approved by 26,223 votes in March 2024. PPIC's September survey found 55% yes and 43% no. No argument against it was filed and no opposition committee exists; the Yes side reports $7.9 million from top donors, including Airbnb, two carpenters' councils, Building a Better California and nonprofit housing developers. This explainer covers where each dollar goes, the veterans' loan bond, the Legislature's power to move money between programs, the cost, the earlier Prop 1s, the money, the argument and the polling.
2026 California propositions master guide: All 14 measures on the November 3 ballot California's November 3, 2026 ballot carries 14 propositions, from an $11.25 billion housing bond to a one-time billionaire tax. This guide covers each measure's rules, its cost according to the Legislative Analyst, who is funding both sides, and where the polls stand as ballots arrive. California Today Mac Douglass | Editor (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/) Proposition 1 would borrow $10 billion for 11 state housing programs and $1.25 billion for veterans' home loans:
The text of the measure (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop1-text-proposed-laws.pdf) has two parts. The first adds Part 16.1 to the Health and Safety Code, creating the Affordable Housing Bond Act Trust Fund of 2026 and authorizing $10 billion in bonds that are "a valid and binding general obligation of the state," with "the full faith and credit of the state … pledged" to repay them. The second adds an article to the Military and Veterans Code authorizing $1.25 billion in veterans' bonds for the farm and home loan program the Department of Veterans Affairs runs under the Veterans' Farm and Home Purchase Act of 1974. Both sets of bonds are sold over time by state finance committees as programs ask for cash, so the state does not borrow the full amount at once.
Section 54054 divides the $10 billion into 11 lines, each assigned to a program already in state law. The Attorney General's summary (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/title-summary.htm) groups them as $5.1 billion for multifamily rental housing, $2.1 billion to acquire, rehabilitate or preserve affordable housing and provide supportive housing, $1.1 billion for homeownership, $1 billion for farmworker, tribal and student housing, $500 million for infrastructure and $200 million for local programs. The LAO's analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/analysis.htm) combines the first two into a single $7.2 billion for affordable multifamily housing. The summary also notes that the money can finance "housing development projects seeking federal tax credits," and the LAO expects most of it to be "used together with other government monies."
Prop 1's $7.2 billion for rental housing runs mostly through the Multifamily Housing Program:

The LAO describes these as "low-interest loans to fund part of the project cost," with units generally reserved for low-income households "for a period of 55 years." Prop 1 adds one condition of its own: at least 10% of the assisted units in each development must be affordable to extremely low-income households.
A further $1.15 billion is set aside for supportive housing, where residents get on-site services such as mental health and substance use counseling. The administering agency must offer capitalized operating subsidy reserves for those units, money set aside up front to cover the gap between what very low-income tenants can pay and what the building costs to run. melessness, and $150 million is reserved for youth housing for current and former foster youth and homeless or at-risk young people, usable only for construction and acquisition and returned to the general program if not committed within three years.
The other two rental lines are about keeping existing housing affordable. The Portfolio Reinvestment Program gets $750 million; its statute, Health and Safety Code section 50606 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=50606), says it exists to "maintain the supply and quality of the affordable rental housing units for which there has already been a significant public investment," including older state-funded buildings whose affordability periods are ending. Another $200 million funds a new program to buy apartments with no rent restrictions and attach long-term affordability limits, "while safeguarding against the displacement of current residents."
The McClatchy editorial board, which recommends (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/article317326136.html) a yes vote, cites Enterprise Community Partners' count of "nearly 40,000 affordable rental homes" that are designed and approved but waiting for financing, and the California Budget & Policy Center's estimate that each state dollar draws $4 from federal, local and private sources. Those are the board's and those groups' figures; the LAO's own estimate is that the bond would subsidize "up to 40,000 multifamily rental units," with the money "used together with other government monies."
Proposition 1 puts $1.1 billion into homeownership through CalHome and CalHFA:
Two lines make up the homeownership money. The CalHome Program receives $600 million for "direct, forgivable loans" to developments with multiple ownership units, including single-family subdivisions, self-help housing where buyers help build their own homes, and manufactured homes. The California Housing Finance Agency receives $500 million for its Home Purchase Assistance Program, which state law (section 51341 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=51341)) aims at making homes "affordable to low- and moderate-income buyers who intend to occupy the homes as their primary residences." That money is continuously appropriated, so CalHFA can spend it without waiting for an annual budget act. The LAO says part of the homeownership money would go to first-time buyers "through loans that generally do not have to be paid back until the home is sold or paid off."
This is a different kind of help from the Proposition 37 (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-proposition-37-guide/) loan on the same ballot. Prop 1's homeownership money is a General Fund-backed subsidy aimed at low- and moderate-income buyers and generally deferred until sale. Prop 37 would have CalHFA sell up to $25 billion in revenue bonds for second mortgages on new homes that buyers repay monthly, with no General Fund backing.
California’s Proposition 37 would let buyers put 3% down on a new home, with a state loan covering the other 17% Proposition 37 would let CalHFA sell $25 billion in revenue bonds and lend buyers of newly built homes up to 17% of the price, so they can put 3% down. The loan is a fixed-rate second mortgage with monthly payments. Here is who qualifies, the county price caps, the cost and who is behind it. California Today Pat Sharyon | Editor (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-proposition-37-guide/) Farmworker, student, tribal and infrastructure money makes up $1.7 billion of Proposition 1:
The Joe Serna, Jr. Farmworker Housing Grant Program gets $450 million for grants and loans to build or rehabilitate housing for agricultural workers and their families, including manufactured housing for families displaced from labor camps and mobile home parks. The LAO estimates the money would fund about 2,500 farmworker units. The Infill Infrastructure Grant Program gets $500 million for the water, sewer, street and park work that high-density affordable and mixed-income projects in already built-up areas need.
The University of California and California State University split $350 million, $175 million each, for new affordable student housing under the terms of Education Code section 17201; the LAO estimates about 1,200 beds. Tribes can apply for $200 million in Tribal Housing Grant Program money "to rebuild and reconstitute their communities." The last $200 million goes to the Local Housing Trust Fund Matching Grant Program for pilot projects testing "innovative, cost-saving approaches to creating or preserving affordable housing," available only to local trust funds that have their own ongoing private or public revenue.
The CalVet home loan bond in Prop 1 is repaid by veterans rather than the General Fund:
The $1.25 billion veterans' portion works differently from the rest of the measure. The state sells bonds to investors and lends the money to eligible veterans to buy homes, farms or mobile homes, and the veterans' mortgage payments flow back to the fund that pays the bondholders. The LAO notes that these payments "have always covered the amount owed on the bonds, meaning the program has always operated at no direct cost to the state," and estimates the new money would help about 2,100 veterans.
They are still general obligation bonds. The text pledges the state's full faith and credit and requires the Director of Finance to transfer any shortfall from the General Fund, which the fund then repays with interest. It also requires an independent public accountant to survey the finances of CalVet's Division of Farm and Home Purchases every year while any of the bonds are outstanding. The last veterans' home loan bond was the $1 billion approved in 2018.
The Legislature could move Proposition 1 money between programs after voters approve it:
The split in the chart is a starting point. Section 54056 lets the Legislature amend the laws governing any of the funded programs "for the purposes of improving the efficiency and effectiveness of those programs," and states that it "may amend this chapter in order to reallocate the proceeds of bonds issued and sold pursuant to this part among the programs to which funds are to be allocated … as necessary to effectively promote the development of affordable housing in this state." A separate clause lets the Business, Consumer Services and Housing Agency, with legislative appropriation, "align or streamline" the programs "to improve efficiency and accelerate the deployment of funds," as long as spending stays within the purposes voters approved.
Unspent money also moves on its own schedule. Most lines revert to the Multifamily Housing Program if not committed by November 3, 2036; the youth housing set-aside, the $200 million acquisition program and the local pilots revert after three years. Agencies may write their own program guidelines without going through the Administrative Procedure Act, the bonds may be issued as taxable bonds and can mature in up to 35 years, and the administering agency must publish an annual report on how the bond money was invested under Health and Safety Code section 50408.
Proposition 1 would cost the General Fund $500 million to $600 million a year for about 25 years:
The LAO estimates repaying the $10 billion housing bond at "$500 million to $600 million annually for about 25 years," or about 0.25% of the General Fund budget. "Since the state has to pay interest on the money it borrows," it adds, "the total cost of the bond would be about 15 percent more (after adjusting for inflation) than if the state paid up front with money it already has." A share of the bond money would cover the administrative costs of the agencies running the programs, and the veterans' bond carries no direct state cost as long as loan payments keep covering it.
The Voter Information Guide's Overview of State Bond Debt (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/voter-info/overview-state-bond-debt.htm) puts Prop 1 alongside the Proposition 38 (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-proposition-38-guide/) immunology research bond as the two General Fund-supported bonds on this ballot, about $1 billion a year combined, against the roughly $6 billion a year the state already pays on about $80 billion of outstanding bonds. For scale, the LAO's analysis of the 2018 housing bond put the cost of its $3 billion General Fund portion at about $170 million a year for 35 years.
California has passed two other bonds called Proposition 1 since 2018 and both funded housing:
Voters have seen the number before. In November 2018, Proposition 1 was a $4 billion veterans and affordable housing bond built on the same template, with $3 billion for state housing programs and $1 billion for CalVet loans. It passed (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2018-general/sov/07-summary.pdf) with 56.2%. In March 2024, Proposition 1 was a $6.38 billion behavioral health bond, which paid for treatment facilities and $2 billion of housing for homeless people with mental health or substance use challenges, just over half of it for veterans, and also changed how the Mental Health Services Act tax is spent. It passed (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2024-primary/ssov/ballot-measure-summary.pdf) with 50.2%, by 26,223 votes out of more than 7.2 million. The LAO counts that 2024 measure as "the last statewide general obligation bond for affordable housing."
